questions.q: A student walks 8 m east, then 3 m west. What is the student's displacement?
questions.explain: Displacement is net change in position: 8 m east − 3 m east = 5 m east. 11 m is the total distance, not displacement.

questions.q: A runner completes exactly one lap of a 400 m track, ending back at the start. What are the distance traveled and the displacement?
questions.explain: Distance is the full path length (400 m). Displacement is net change in position — since the runner ends where they started, displacement is 0.

questions.q: A hiker walks 6 km north, then 8 km east. What is the magnitude of the displacement? (Total distance walked is 14 km.)
questions.explain: Displacement is a vector, so use the Pythagorean theorem on the two perpendicular legs: sqrt(6² + 8²) = sqrt(100) = 10 km. Distance (14 km) is not the same as displacement magnitude.

questions.q: A car speeds up from 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s, with constant acceleration. What is the car's average velocity over that time?
questions.explain: For constant acceleration, average velocity = (v_i + v_f)/2 = (0+20)/2 = 10 m/s — not the final velocity.

questions.q: A car travels 100 km east in 2 hours, then 100 km west in 2 hours, ending back where it started. What are its average speed and average velocity for the whole 4-hour trip?
questions.explain: Average speed = total distance/time = 200 km/4 h = 50 km/h. Average velocity = displacement/time = 0 km/4 h = 0, since the car ends up where it started.

questions.q: A car's speedometer reads 60 km/h at one specific moment while driving. This reading is measuring:
options: Average velocity over the whole trip
Average speed over the last hour
questions.explain: A speedometer shows the speed at that instant — instantaneous speed — not an average over any time interval, and not a vector (velocity).

questions.q: A car moving in the +x direction has a negative acceleration. What is definitely true?
options: The car's velocity and acceleration point in opposite directions
questions.explain: The only thing guaranteed is that acceleration (−x) is opposite the car's velocity (+x). Whether that means 'slowing down' depends on knowing velocity's direction, which we do here — but the general, always-true fact is about the signs being opposite.

questions.q: An object moving in the −x direction has acceleration also in the −x direction (same sign). What is happening to its speed?
questions.explain: When velocity and acceleration share the same sign (same direction), the object speeds up — regardless of whether that direction is positive or negative.

questions.q: Which statement about acceleration is always true?
options: Positive acceleration always means speeding up
Negative acceleration always means slowing down
The sign of acceleration alone doesn't tell you if an object speeds up or slows down — you need to compare it to velocity's sign
Acceleration is always in the same direction as velocity
questions.explain: Speeding up vs. slowing down depends on whether acceleration and velocity have the same or opposite signs — not on the sign of acceleration by itself.

questions.q: You know initial velocity, final velocity, and displacement, but NOT time. Which kinematic equation solves directly for acceleration?
questions.explain: v_f² = v_i² + 2aΔx is the only one of the four kinematic equations that doesn't contain time — exactly what's needed when t is unknown.

questions.q: You know initial velocity, acceleration, and time, but not final velocity. Which equation lets you find displacement directly, without first computing v_f?
questions.explain: Δx = v_i t + ½at² uses only v_i, a, and t — exactly the three knowns here — to solve for displacement in one step.

questions.q: A car starts at rest and accelerates at 4 m/s² for 5 s. How far does it travel?
On a velocity-time graph, the AREA under the curve between two times represents:
questions.explain: Area under a v–t graph = displacement. Slope of a v–t graph is acceleration — these two are frequently swapped by mistake.

questions.q: On a position-time graph, a straight line with a steep positive slope represents:
questions.explain: Slope of a position-time graph is velocity. A steep straight (constant-slope) line means a large, constant velocity — not acceleration, which would require a curved x-t line.

questions.q: A velocity-time graph is a horizontal line above the t-axis (not at zero). What does this tell you?
options: Velocity is zero; acceleration is constant
Velocity is constant (nonzero); acceleration is zero
Velocity is increasing; acceleration is constant
Both velocity and acceleration are zero
questions.explain: A flat, nonzero line on a v–t graph means velocity isn't changing — constant nonzero velocity, and therefore zero slope, i.e., zero acceleration.

questions.q: A ball is thrown upward at 12 m/s from ground level (ignore air resistance). What is its speed when it returns to the same height it was thrown from?
options: It depends on the mass of the ball
questions.explain: By symmetry of free fall, an object returns to its launch height with the same speed it left, just directed downward. Mass doesn't affect free-fall motion.

questions.q: A heavy bowling ball and a light tennis ball are dropped from the same height at the same time (ignore air resistance). Which hits the ground first?
options: They land at the same time
questions.explain: In free fall (no air resistance), acceleration is g for every object regardless of mass, so both fall together and land at the same time.

questions.q: An object is dropped from rest and falls for 2.0 s. How far does it fall? (g = 9.8 m/s²)
A ball is thrown straight up. At the exact top of its path, what is true about its velocity and acceleration?
options: Both velocity and acceleration are zero
Velocity is zero; acceleration is still −g
Velocity is at its maximum; acceleration is zero
Velocity is zero; acceleration is also zero momentarily, then returns to −g
questions.explain: Velocity is momentarily zero at the peak, but gravity never stops acting — acceleration is −g for the entire flight, including at the top.

questions.q: A ball thrown straight up takes 1.5 s to reach its highest point. How long does the entire trip (up, then back down to launch height) take?
questions.explain: Free fall is symmetric: time up equals time down (when launch and landing heights match), so total time = 2 × 1.5 s = 3.0 s.

questions.q: At the instant a ball thrown upward reaches its peak height, which statement is correct?
options: The net force on it is zero
Gravity is still pulling down on it with full force
questions.explain: Gravity acts continuously on the ball throughout its flight, including at the peak — it does not switch off just because velocity is momentarily zero.

questions.q: An object moves with constant velocity. What is its acceleration?
questions.explain: If velocity isn't changing, Δv = 0 over any Δt, so a = Δv/Δt = 0.

questions.q: An object's velocity-time graph is a horizontal line at −5 m/s (constant velocity in the negative direction). What is its acceleration?
options: Cannot be determined without more info
questions.explain: A constant velocity — even a negative constant — always means zero acceleration. The value of the velocity itself is irrelevant to whether it's changing.

questions.q: If an object's acceleration is zero at some instant, does that mean its velocity is also zero at that instant?
options: No — zero acceleration only means velocity isn't changing at that instant; it can be any nonzero constant value
Only if it started at rest
questions.explain: Zero acceleration means velocity is momentarily constant — it says nothing about the value of that velocity, which can be large, small, positive, or negative, just not changing.
